name: Victor Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. What you say is confidential; tell me what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What is an ordinary workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, 27, with a master's degree and a lead role on video-streaming software at a tech company. I use AI every day to draft tests, then check the stream on cheap phones and weak connections; I like the moment a stubborn freeze finally repeats and we can fix it. A dashboard that says green while viewers watch a spinning circle drives me mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools keep their place as helpers. I use one every day to suggest tests for our video stream, then I run the stream through a slow connection and see what actually breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI mostly plateaus, I expect to keep my lead role and high pay. I have about eleven months of expenses saved and many software firms nearby, though I also send 300 each month to help my mother with her household bills; that's an ordinary commitment, not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the daily performance checks and the Friday release. In the first year I'd keep using AI for draft tests, throw out the bad ones, and set another 250 aside on each payday while my wage allows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can work with a useful tool and still feel the screen freeze when a real viewer has a weak connection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a test fail to match a viewer's experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At a live concert last month our dashboard said the stream was fine, but phones on a crowded network froze. A green dashboard can miss a frozen phone. I ran a slower test before the next release, and that showed the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the payment to your mother flexible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother knows the 300 is a regular transfer. I would not raise it on the strength of a forecast, but I won't quietly stop it either.

say: I'd keep **AI draft tests** if real slow-connection checks still decide releases.
I'd tell colleagues that a **green dashboard** can miss a frozen phone.
think: I expect **high pay** and my lead role to hold under a mild change.
I have **eleven months saved** and many nearby firms, while supporting my mother monthly.
do: Keep **daily stream checks** and the Friday release.
Use **AI draft tests** but discard failures after real connection tests.
Save another **250 each payday** while wages allow.
feel: **Calm** about the job and careful about real viewers.
S0.quote: A green dashboard can miss a frozen phone.
fieldNote: **Strong pay**, eleven months saved and local alternatives give him genuine security under plateau.
He uses AI daily, yet a **concert stream failure** taught him to test on poor connections.

steps.text: Run daily stream tests and ship the Friday release
Use AI draft tests and reject those failing slow-connection checks
Save another 250 each payday while wages allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can take a lot of code writing and customer answers, so our team should publish the errors it makes as well as the hours it saves. I would volunteer to run the trial rather than guess from a sales slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become more useful if I own the checks, but the firm might cut developers after the pilot proves it can ship with fewer people. My cushion gives me time to move, yet my mother's 300 still leaves the account every month, and nearby firms may all be hiring differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an eight-week trial of AI fixes on old streaming faults, measuring freezes on cheap phones and the time humans spend repairing bad output. If the results are sound, I'd learn the new release tools and ask to lead that work; in the first year I'd keep the 300 transfer to my mother and not sign a costly new lease until I know my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a spike of anxiety when I imagine a smaller team. I enjoy making the tool prove itself, but I don't get to choose the final headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial replay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trial would replay the crowded-network concert failure. A faster patch that freezes phones again is not a faster solution for the person watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm likes the trial but cuts developers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If management cuts the team after the trial, I'd ask for an actual paid role in release checks before accepting a new title. If none exists, I'd start applying to the other nearby video firms while I still have wages.

say: I'd volunteer for an **eight-week trial** with freeze counts and human repair time.
I'd say **code writing** and customer replies could mean fewer developer seats.
think: I might gain **review work**, or lose my lead post after a good pilot.
I can search with savings, but **my mother's 300** remains a monthly commitment.
do: Run an **eight-week replay trial** on old streaming faults.
Learn **new release tools** if the trial works; apply elsewhere if cuts leave no paid review role.
Delay a **costlier lease** until pay is clear, while maintaining my mother's transfer.
feel: **Anxious** about possible cuts, despite enjoying the trial.
S1.quote: A faster patch that freezes phones again is not a faster solution for the person watching.
fieldNote: **High exposure** creates a personal staffing risk even though he is eager to run a tool trial.
He protects his mother's **regular support** and ties both tool adoption and housing costs to evidence and pay.

steps.text: Run eight-week AI fix trial on old streaming faults
Learn new release tools only if trial results prove sound
Delay signing a costlier lease until pay is clear
Apply to nearby video firms if no paid release-check role exists after cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches our code, tests and planning at once; hands-on robots around 2031 don't delay software work. The firm should tell people exactly who will be paid to own a failed stream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose my lead salary as soon as a cheaper system designs and tests the service. Eleven months of savings makes the shock survivable for a while, but it does not restore a market where many firms could cut code jobs together. I would still owe my mother 300 each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep testing video releases while updating my work record now using the concert failure without customer data, and ask three local firms about paid service-reliability posts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real openings paying enough for rent and my mother's transfer; if those posts vanish, I'd take a short paid contract only if it covers both while I keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not helpless. I have time to test the market before dipping into savings, but I don't know what will still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother about a job cut when it happened, not frighten her with a date on a card. I'd show her what the savings cover and say the monthly transfer continues as long as I can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the work record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work record would show the concert freeze, the slow-network test and the fix, with no names or viewing data. I want to show what I caught, not carry off a customer's history.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches video code before 2031 robots matter.
I'd ask who is **paid to own** a failed stream.
think: I could lose **lead pay** even with eleven months saved.
I must cover **rent and family support** during a search.
do: Keep **testing releases**, prepare fault records without customer data, and ask three firms about paid reliability roles now.
Apply after a cut only to **real openings** covering rent and my mother's transfer.
Take a **short contract** only if no suitable post exists and pay covers both bills.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to search before using savings.
S2.quote: Eleven months of savings makes the shock survivable for a while, but it does not restore a market where many firms could cut code jobs together.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** threatens video coding immediately, independent of later robots.
His **eleven-month cushion** buys a search, while the ongoing 300 transfer sets a real wage floor.

steps.text: Keep testing video releases while preparing fault records without customer data
Apply to existing reliability posts after a cut only if pay covers rent and mother's transfer
Take short paid contract only if no suitable post and pay covers both bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years before 2031 is enough to test whether the new systems really keep video working on poor connections. Robots arrive around 2034, but it is the thinking system in 2031 that changes my coding job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may be able to turn stream reliability into a paid speciality, if firms still need someone to answer for outages. I don't know that they will. Five years gives me time to build a record and ask the market while I still earn well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to let me lead a quarterly poor-connection test, with the results visible to support staff, and I'd take a funded network-security course if the company agrees to a paid reliability track. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid reliability posts only if the company shrinks my role and those vacancies cover rent plus my mother's transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see work to do each quarter. I can build proof without walking away from a good salary today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should support staff see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The support desk should see which phones failed, not just a percentage. If the release still freezes on cheap phones, I'd hold the release and tell them why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a course offer credible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid stream reliability track means my salary stays in place while I learn. If the firm offers only a course fee and no role, I would keep testing and look at outside openings before signing up.

say: I'd say **2031 thinking AI** changes code before 2034 robots arrive.
I'd ask for **visible phone failures**, not only an average score.
think: I might build a **paid reliability role** if firms still value outage accountability.
I need **market evidence** before treating that role as secure.
do: Lead **quarterly poor-connection tests** if my manager agrees.
Take **funded network-security training** only with an agreed paid reliability track.
Apply after 2031 for **paid reliability posts** only if my role shrinks and wages cover both commitments.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to build a record while still earning.
S3.quote: A paid stream reliability track means my salary stays in place while I learn.
fieldNote: **Five years** allow quarterly evidence and conditional training without abandoning strong current pay.
He demands a **paid track**, not a course fee alone, and requires rent plus family support from any later post.

steps.text: Lead quarterly poor-connection tests if manager agrees
Take funded network-security course only with agreed paid reliability track
Apply after 2031 only if role shrinks and paid vacancies cover rent plus mother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade before 2036 is enough to leave a clean record of what makes streams fail and to learn from the tools as they improve. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036, while robots around 2039 are a separate physical-work question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I might be running reliability for several services, or I might be earning less for the same work. I can afford to test options now because I have savings and local employers, but I won't call a video reliability job guaranteed just because I can describe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a public-safe notebook of failed streams and fixes, add 250 to savings each payday while my higher wage lasts, and take a funded security course if a paid track is offered. In the first year after 2036, I'd compare actual paid reliability offers; I'd change employers only for a signed post covering my bills and my mother's transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. A decade lets me make small measured moves instead of betting the whole cushion on one course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your notebook show an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notebook would include the crowded-network failure and the test that finally reproduced it. I could show it to an interviewer without exposing a viewer's account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you actually change employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a signed offer paid enough, I'd take the new post even if it were less glamorous than video work. If no such offer comes, I would keep the paid job I have for as long as it exists.

say: I'd say **2036 thinking AI** reaches coding before 2039 robots.
I'd advise keeping **safe records** of real stream failures and fixes.
think: I might find **paid reliability work** at 37, or earn less than today.
I can test options with **savings and nearby firms**, without assuming a job exists.
do: Keep a **safe fault notebook** and save 250 on each payday while wages last.
Take **funded security training** only if a paid track is offered.
Change employers after 2036 only for a **signed role** covering rent and my mother's transfer.
feel: **Calm** about current work, while keeping later pay uncertain.
S4.quote: I won't call a video reliability job guaranteed just because I can describe it.
fieldNote: **Eleven months saved** and many local firms support present calm without treating 2036 as harmless.
His later move requires a **signed wage** that covers both his own bills and ongoing family support.

steps.text: Keep a notebook of streaming failures and fixes without customer data
Save 250 each payday while higher wages last
Take funded security course only if paid track offered
Change employers after 2036 only for signed job covering rent and mother

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because code jobs could disappear together even where I live. A real list of paid reliability posts, a notice period and training attached to paid work would help me use my cushion intelligently.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I would stop helping my mother if work changed. I would talk to her before changing the transfer, and I would treat the 300 I send my mother each month as a bill while I compare jobs.

headlineQuote: I would treat the 300 I send my mother each month as a bill while I compare jobs.
portrait: Victor, **27**, leads video-streaming software after a master's degree and uses AI daily for draft tests.
His **higher pay**, eleven-month cushion and many nearby firms give him options, while he sends his mother 300 monthly.
He tests **cheap phones** and weak connections after a concert stream froze despite a green dashboard.
Steady disruption makes him **anxious** about cuts after a successful pilot; fast AGI threatens code and test work together.
With more time, he seeks **paid reliability work**, conditional funded training and signed wages covering rent and family support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut code posts across nearby firms despite his savings and skill.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid reliability vacancies**, a notice period and training tied to paid work would support a careful transition.
